description.narrative: Oxfam in Uganda with support from GAC conducted a Capacity Assessment Tool for Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights (CAT4SRHR) in 2022 for its stand-up project partners in Uganda including Reproductive Health Uganda (RHU). The training objectives were to provideoverview on SRHR, values clarification, and review foundational concepts to working on SRHR, from a rights-based approach, familiarize participants with the CAT4SRHR, how to guide Stand Up partners through the process, and develop a capacity-strengthening action plan and to provide participants with an opportunity to practice facilitating the CAT4SRHR training. After the training, participants were tasked with replicating the same training in their respective organizations with all their membersand implement an action plan drawn during the training based on capacity needs. It is based on this premise that RHU is to be supported with funds to implementthe CAT4SRHR action plan.

participating-org.narrative:
The history of Family Planning in Uganda dates back to the 1950’s and is closely linked to the visit of Ms. Edith Gates – ExecutiveDirector of Pathfinder International (standing). Ms Gates was visiting sub Saharan Africa to explore the possibilities of introducing modern family planning associations in African countries. She urged progressive Asian and African women of Mothers’ Union to forman association that would advocate for Family Planning. To have the impact they wanted, the women decided to transform this club oflike-minded individuals into something more. That is when they founded the FPAU in 1957 with the first clients being attended at the Agha Khan Health Centre.
In 1963, after six years in operation, FPAU was registered as an NGO under the National Council of Voluntary Social Services. The Association opened its first clinic in 1964, and the number of those seeking family planning services tooka steady rise. FPAU BECOMES A MEMBER OF INTERNATIONAL PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION (IPPF) In 1966, amidst funding struggles, FPAU was registered as a member of IPPF. This development opened doors for further financial assistance. In May 1968, the 21st World health Assembly, under resolution WHA 21.43, recognized family planning as an importantcomponent of basic health care service. This global proclamation made many national governments including Uganda to start giving serious consideration to family planning. SURVIVAL IN TROUBLED TIMES The 1970’s will remain etched in the minds of supporters of family planning as the most difficult period. When Idi Amin took control of the country after a military coup, he banned family planning, arguing it was against African Culture. Consequently, the government did not accept FPAU to open and run clinicsin government hospitals and prohibited tutors and lecturers from giving FP lectures to medical students. It is during this troubled period that the total fertility rate and maternal mortality increasedto levels that threatened attainment of safe motherhood and threw the population economic balance into disarray. As the Association struggled to remain, the reputation of the country also suffered a great deal; donors were hesitant to support FPAU programs in such hostile environment. Only IPPF stood withthe Association, sustaining it during these trying times. Within the organization, the difficult times also saw it experience some of the worst managerial and administrative challenges. However, despite all this and due to the resilience of FP advocatesthe Association registered great success through its Advocacy efforts which led the Ministry of Health to accept child spacing as an essential component of primary healthcare. In 1975, the Ministry instructed all of its medical units to work with FPAU and in collaboration with IPPF, FPAU influenced Makerere University to start a course on population research and demography. LOOKING TO THE FUTURE: CHANGE OF NAME FROM FPAU TO RHU 2007, After a sterling performance since its formation 50 yearsago, the FPAUstarted the journey in its next half of the century by changing of its name from FPAU to Reproductive Health Uganda (RHU) in line with the organisation’s current goals, objectives and realities on ground. The change of name was necessitated by the shift in paradigm from mere family planning to the broader and holistic SRHR that the organisation fully embraced since the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) in 1994.
2. ACHIEVEMENTS Reproductive Health Uganda Key Achievements 1. Recognized Leader in SRHR Media Advocacy In 2024, Akina Mama wa Afrika recognized RHU as one of the top contributors driving Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) conversations in Uganda. This was highlighted in their annual report assessingmedia coverage on SRHR. RHU’s proactive approach through webinars, stakeholder consultations, and robust online campaigns positioned the organization as a national and global thought leader in SRHR knowledge sharing and digital advocacy.
2. Championing the SRHR–Climate Change Nexus Cognizant of the impact of climate change on vulnerable populations, RHU has taken a frontline role in integrating SRHR into climate change adaptation efforts. • RHU played an instrumental role in the development and launch of the Kasese District Climate Change Adaptation Plan, ensuring that SRHR was central to community resilience strategies. • At the national level, the Ministry of Health acknowledged RHU’s contributions during the official launch of the Climate andHealth National Adaptation Plan (2025–2030). • Regionally, the Kasese District Local Government awarded RHU for its role in building a climate-resilient health system and community. This recognition underscores RHU’s pioneering efforts to spotlight health—particularly SRHR—as a critical aspect of climate change adaptation.
2. Community-Led Infrastructure for SRHR Access RHU recorded a significant milestone in community-led resource mobilisation in Luwero District, where volunteers led efforts to construct a new, spacious clinic in Wobulenzi Town Council. This initiative has greatly improved access to SRHR services for youth, women, and men across the greater Luwero area, demonstrating RHU’s commitment to community ownership and sustainability.
3. Innovation Through Digital Health and Service Delivery Transformation Recognizing the transformative power of technology, RHU has integrated digital innovations into service delivery, research, and communication. • The organization has strengthened its service delivery structure to enhance accessibility, efficiency, and quality. • Future plans include clinic redesigns, technology-driven health services, and adoption of health insurance models to meet emerging needs. • RHU’s new Strategic Plan (2025–2030) places digital innovation, youth-centered services, and private sector collaboration at its core, ensuringthe organization remains future-ready and sustainable. 4. Strengthening Partnerships for Sustainability In line with its commitmentto sustainability, RHU has significantly expanded partnerships with private sector actors, especially to promote SRHR in workplaces. These partnerships are critical in reaching underserved populations, advocating for safeguarding policies, and creating SRHR-friendlyenvironments within the formal employment sector. 5. National Recognition for Family Planning and Safe Motherhood
RHU was honored with the National Safe Motherhood Award 2023 during the second edition of the National Safe Motherhood Conference. The award, under the “Outstanding Contribution to Safe Motherhood – Family Planning” NGO category, affirms RHU’s dedication to improving maternal health outcomes through access to quality family planning services.
3. INSTITUTIONAL PURPOSE Mission:To champion and sustainablyprovide capacity building, research evidence, high quality rights based SRHR information and services, with a special focus on young people. Institutional objectives: 1. Enhance Gender Programming and Meaningful Youth InclusiveParticipation in Institutional Structures, Systems, and Operation 2. Leverage partnerships, networking and communications to influence the SRHR ecosystem and enhance RHU’s identity and visibility 3. Provide quality people-centred SRHR services and information especially to young people, vulnerable groups and those in humanitarian settings 4. Leverage innovations, knowledge, learning and evidence to influence the SRHR ecosystem 5. Strengthen RHU organisational capacity to deliver on its mandate, including strengthening capacity of actors for sustainable SRHR, youth programming, advocacy, service delivery, leadership and management
Field(s) of activity: What are the principal thematic and geographic areas in which the organization works? Coverage RHU has 18 branches (currently operates 16 clinics) spread across all sub-regions of Uganda. The organisation has made a significant contribution in the area of SRHR. RHU’s plans to enhance SRHR in Uganda and contribute to regional and global advocacy efforts. RHU’s Strategy provides approaches to transform the SRHR ecosystem. RHU has structured its operations around five interconnected thematic areas, which will serve as the foundation. These areas are: gender and youth-centred programming and involvement, advocacy, communications, partnerships and networking; re-invention of client-centred SRHR medical services; research, innovations, knowledge management, monitoring and evaluation, institutional sustainability. They are aligned with the four pillars ofIPPF, which focus on advancing the sexuality agenda, prioritising people-centred care, fostering solidarity for change, and supporting the federation. In essence, these thematic areas reflect RHU’s shift in programming focus to better serve the SRHR needs of the broader population, with particular attention given to vulnerable groups such as young people, women, key populations (KPs), persons with disabilities (PWDs), orphans and vulnerable children (OVC), populations in humanitarian settings, the elderly, and the poor. These groups are identified in the Third National Development Plan (2020) as residing in areas with service delivery inequalities and facing additional challenges due to the effects of climate change, political conflicts, negative cultural norms, among others. By transforming the SRHR ecosystem, RHU aims to shape laws, policies, and norms through local and global advocacy actions. This will require strengthening its research and innovations components, as well as positioning itself as a leading agency in SRHR training and capacity building. RHU will continue to fulfill its core mandate of providing medical services and SRHR information to create a lasting impact. The first four thematic areas primarily focus on RHU’s interventions for external stakeholders, while the last one concentrates on the organisation’s internal development. Each thematic area includes critical pathways (CPs), which are the key interventions that RHU needs to prioritise in order to achieve its overall goal. These pathways will serve asthe basis for developing detailed activities to implement the strategy on an annual basis.
Over the past decade, there has been a significant emphasis on SRHR as a crucial driver of global economic development. Young people have experienced increased freedoms, opportunities, and the ability to make decisions and shape their own lives. However, progress has been uneven, with notable variations in different countries and population subcategories. The following narratives elaborateon some of the shifts in focus that RHU hasundergone. 1. Gender and Youth Centred Programming and Involvement RHU, since its establishment, has been dedicated to empowering youth by offering them opportunities, resources, and platforms to activelyparticipate in decision-making processes. The organisation facilitates the implementation of initiatives that have a positive impact on the lives of young people. Positioned as a youth centred organisation, RHU adheres to the principle of “nothing for uswithout us.” Recognising that harnessing the demographic dividend of the country requires a critical investment in young people SRHR, RHU emphasises the importance of their meaningful participation andinclusion in achieving this goal. RHU recognises thevast potential of young people, yet they are often left out in decision making processes, planning, programming and governance. Cognisant of the Agenda 2030, of leaving no one behind, RHU intends to continue investing in nurturing the leadership skills, personal and professional development of young people, and amplifying their voices. RHU is committed to strengthening institutional systems, structures, and programmes to sustain and enhance meaningful and inclusive youthparticipation (MIYP) across all its operations. This strategic approach aims to create a lasting impact by ensuring that the voicesand contributions of young people are integral to the organisation’s mission and objectives. 2. Advocacy, Communications, Partnerships and Networking I. Advocacy The advocacy function is intended to enable RHU to address the existing challenges and opportunities. There is a need to take advantage of the current positive ‘policy window’ that presents RHU with opportunities to make a positive impact towards transforming the SRHR ecosystem. The SRHR indices in Uganda are poor and some of them have stagnated over time, whichhas had a negative impact on the population, there is need to intensify policy and budgetary advocacy, and strategic communication.Meanwhile,the socio-cultural set up surrounding SRHR issues in Uganda is fairly conservative, largely affected by religious and cultural beliefs and norms, leading to myths and misconceptions related to the issue of modern contraception, sex and sexuality education, contraceptive use. Gender equality, sexual gender-based violence, key and priority populations are still taboo topics for discussion in public. In addition, the continental, East African region and global SRH policy frameworks such as the Maputo Plan of Action, Africa Health Strategy, Abuja Declaration, ICPD and SDGs provide additional windows of opportunity. They call for repositioning ofSRHR and universal access to reproductive health to accelerate development. However, these protocols exist amidst significant resistance. This calls for concerted actions guided by strategic partnerships, networking and advocacy. II. Communications RHU communication target both internal and external audiences to increase visibility of SRHR, demystify myths and misconceptions, and change negative attitudes towards SRHR. RHU intends to communicate to increase visibility and strengthen the identity of the organisation. The purpose of communication will focus on increasing access to accurate SRHR information, enhancing RHU’s identity and visibility nationally and internationally. RHU will strengthen social behavioural change communication efforts to reverse negative social norms. III.Partnerships and Networking RHU intends to revitalise strategic partnerships and networking. This will boost RHU’s efforts to transform the SRHR ecosystem in Uganda and beyond. RHU is cognisant of the fact that successful advocacy is hinged on partnerships and networks with like-minded individuals and organisations/institutions to canvass the required support and strong voices necessary in influencing policy- you can never do it alone and succeed. Likewise, the organisation will collaborate and network with a vision to improve the delivery of social services and catalysing transformative social change. Partnership brings together institutional capabilities and human resources in form of skills, experiences and ideas to tackle common advocacy issues that are often beyond the capacity of a single organisation or group. 3. Re-invention of Client -centred SRHR Service Delivery RHU intend to contribute to strengthening of the healthcare system. the aim is to ensure a high standard of health for all individuals in the country, promoting healthy and productive lives. RHU will continue delivering on her core mandate of providing SRHR services and information to priority populations particularly adolescents and young people. RHU operates a network of 16 own clinics, over 200 public partner facilities and 50LIFEPLUS social franchise private clinics across different regions of Uganda. However, these clinics have been providing general SRHR services without specialising in specific areas that cater to the growing and diverse needs of service users. As a result, the capacity of the clinics to attract more service users has been limited, leading to financial challenges in their management and sustainability. The scope of SRH has in majority of its clinics been limited to contraceptives, cancer screening and PAC, leaving out a big group of clients with safe motherhood needs including antenatal, deliveries and postnatal care. RHU intends to upgrade her laboratory services to meet the technological advancements and evolving service demands of the clientele. In addition, RHU will focus on modernising the health facilities to be able to attract medical insurance services. To enhance the impact and sustainability of RHU’s services, it is crucial to prioritize the specialization of clinics based on the specific needs of service users. By adaptingand expanding their service package, the clinics can better attract and serve a wider range of individuals, ultimately making their management more financially viable. Additionally, investing in upgrading laboratory services to meet current technological standards will ensure accurate and efficient diagnostic capabilities, enhancing the quality of care provided. 4. Addressing SRHR in Humanitarian Settings The enjoyment of SRH rights is greatly influenced by stable conditions. However, during humanitarian crises, various factors further impede access to and utilisation of SRHR services. These factors encompass harmful gender norms, poverty, and the lack of basic services like education and sexual and reproductive healthcare. In response to thissituation, RHU aims to boost its provision of SRHR clinical services to refugee settings. This initiative specifically targets the needs of this vulnerable population subgroup. The boosting will involve the establishment of static clinics as well as conducting outreaches, both tailored to address the specificservice delivery requirements in these settings. 5. Focus on Climate Crisis By 2030, it is anticipated that two-thirds of IPPF clients will reside in countries where inequalities have worsened, with a significant portion of this increase attributed to the climatecrisis (IPPF strategic Plan 2028). The shifting population dynamics, particularly in terms of growth, will inevitably impact resource utilisation. Consequently, the effects on the climatewill be most profoundly experienced by future generations, especially young people. In recognition of these challenges, the NDPIII underscores the urgent need to address population dynamics as a crucial component in tackling the consequences of climate change. This strategic approach is vital for achieving improved household incomes and enhancing the overall quality of life for the population. Additionally, the plan highlights the perils associated with climate change, including regional conflicts, population migrations, and the resultant influx of refugees, all of which exert pressure on resourceutilisation, thereby diminishing the quality of life for the broader population. This underscores the significance of addressing the SRHR needs of the population. By doing so, we can actively contribute to nurturing a thriving society that prioritises the well-being and quality of life for all. 6. Research, Innovations, Knowledge Management and M<(>&<)>E Influencing the SRHR ecosystem will require generating evidence on what works best to address the dynamic needs of communities, especially young people. Over the past seven years, there has been a remarkable increase in the scope and momentum of evidence related to SRHR. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that there are still notable research and data gaps in our comprehension of this vital field. These gaps hinder our understanding of various aspects, including the reasons behind limited access to SRHR services, the effectiveness of different interventions,the unexplored contexts of service delivery in humanitarian crisis settings, strategies for scaling up and reaching marginalised communities, including young people, and optimal collaboration with sectors like social development, health, and education. Evidence takes various forms, such as operational research, evaluations, and compelling stories of significant change, lessons learned, qualitative and quantitative research, case studies, and ongoing discussions among practitioners. Furthermore, valuableinsights can also be gleaned from programme and policies implemented in other sectors. To strengthen the SRHR ecosystem, it is imperative to build upon the existing evidence and address these research and data gaps. By doing so, we can develop comprehensive strategies that effectively respond to the SRHR needs of young people. Innovations With the rapidly changing SRHR environment, innovations in programme design and implementation is crucial ensuring that the right approaches/ models and tools are used in delivering the desired organisational aspirations and mission. RHU intends to invest and facilitate the development of innovative initiatives and ventures for delivering information and services related to SRHR, especially targeting young people. 7. Institutional Sustainability RHU, similar to other non-governmental organisations (NGOs), has previously functioned as a standard non-profit organisation, consistently implementingits programmes and achieving results across all core programme areas. The organisation has invested a significant amount of time infundraising, and now intends to strengthen strategies to attract more funds required to support the execution of the strategic plan. It is worth noting that RHU plans to strengthen its internal fundraising, which will in turn lead to achieving its investment plan. RHU intends to operationalise its Business Plan, to effectively align with the organisation’s operational and programmatic resource requirements. To transform the SRHR Ecosystem, itis crucial to adopt a well-considered approach to revenue generation that can sustain and expand RHU’s programmes while increasing the impact. This necessitates the development of a funding model, business plan, and investment strategy that provide a level of stability and generate the necessary revenue to foster growth and programme delivery.RHU’s funding model aims to facilitate the scaling up of programmes in the face of diminishing donor funding, reduce dependence on donors, and enhance financial sustainability. 8. Training and Capacity Building To transform the SRHR ecosystem, it’s critical to improve investment in human capital development that can support effective delivery of SRHR services, provision of information, and provide strategic leadership and management, boost advocacy efforts and youth-centred programming. In addition, to overcome societal norms that hinder women and girls and promote transformative feminist action, it is crucial to capacitate key stakeholders and empower communitystructures. It is vital to enhance the capacity of influential individuals within community structures, such as religious, cultural, and political leaders, who can promote a shared agenda for transforming the SRHR ecosystem.
